_exec_summary.SummaryText:
This Risk Management Plan Executive Summary was developed pursuant to Section 2745.3 of the California Accidental Release Prevention (CalARP) Program codified by Title 19, California Code of Regulations (CCR), Division 2, and Chapter 4.5. The purpose of this Executive Summary is to provide a brief description of certain elements of the Risk Management Plan that has been implemented at the City of California City Wastewater Treatment Plant, 10835 Nelson Drive, California City, CA 93505. The objectives of the California Accidental Release Prevention Program are to prevent the accidental release of certain regulated substances, minimize the risk to the community, and promote communication between the facility and emergency response personnel.

1.0 ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION
City of California City has a long-standing commitment to worker and public safety.  This commitment is demonstrated by the resources invested in accident prevention, such as personnel training and consideration of safety in the design, operation, and maintenance of the covered processes.  City of California City policy is to implement reasonable controls to prevent foreseeable releases of regulated substances.

2.0 STATIONARY SOURCE AND REGULATED SUBSTANCE
The main operation of City of California Citys Wastewater Treatment Plant is an extended air, tertiary wastewater treatment plant with a maximum design capability of 1.5 million gallons per day and an instantaneous flow of 3.0 million gallons per day. The current inflow average is 950,000 gallons per day. Preliminary treatment consists of two submersible chopper pumps in a wet well, an automatic bar screen with washer compactor and flow indicator. The secondary treatment consists of two aeration basins with surface aerators, two secondary clarifiers with a return activated sludge/waste activated sludge lift station and chopper pumps. Tertiary treatment consists of a filter influent pump station, flocculation unit, up-flow sand filters, and a

chlorine contact chamber with a 2-hour contact time. In principle, the control system monitors flow downstream of the filter influent lift station to correctly meter the injection of chlorine at the in-flow of the chlorine contact tank. Chlorine is stored in 1-ton D.O.T. cylinders in the chemical feed building.  A maximum of two cylinders are connected to the injection system with one cylinder in operation. Chlorine gas is extracted from the cylinders under vacuum by virtue of chlorine vapor pressure and the venturi created by the chlorine solution eductor valve or the mechanical injection submersible pump located at the in-flow of the chlorine contact tank. 
City of California City Wastewater Treatment Plant uses the following chemicals in amounts that exceed the regulatory threshold for certain regulatory defined processes including:

Chlorine

3.0 HAZARD ASSESSMENT SUMMARY
Worst-Case Release Scenario Results Summary for Toxics
Process 1 WCR Scenario Description: The worst-case scenario for chlorine assumes a rupture and release of the entire contents of 2000 lbs of D.O.T. cylinder in the Chemical Feed Building, containing 1900 lbs of chlorine. The tanks are administratively controlled to hold 95% maximum capacity. As per the guidance of RMP in determining quantity for the worst-case scenario, the largest quantity should be determined, considering administrative controls rather than the absolute capacity of the vessel or pipe. The air temperature used in the simulation is 77°F according to the required parameter for worst-case modeling (40 CFR 68.22  Ambient temperature/humidity (68.22)). This guidance assumes 25°C (77°F) and 50 percent humidity. For other models for toxic substances, you must use the highest daily maximum temperature and average humidity for the site during the past three years. Moreover, an enclosure was considered a mitigation measure since D.O.T. cylinders are stored in an airtight structure and for a release of toxic gas in an enclosed. Usin

g the parameters mandated by regulations through the RMP*Comp program, this worst-case release has a total of 1900 lbs of chlorine released into the atmosphere with the potential to traverse a 2.2-mile radius from the point of release and the potential to affect the population of 4,811 people.

4.0 ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION PROGRAM AND CHEMICAL-SPECIFIC PREVENTION STEPS
As part of the implementation of this Risk Management Program, key Prevention Program elements were implemented by City of California Ci

ty to manage process safety issues associated with the covered processes. In addition, common industry standards, policies, and procedures are currently utilized to ensure safe practices are being performed.
City of California City Wastewater Treatment Plant CalARP Prevention Program 3 elements for the toxic substances, chlorine, include: 
Common Elements of CalARP Prevention Program 3
Process Safety Information
Process Hazard Analysis
Operating Procedures
Training
Mechanical Integrity
Management of Change
Pre-Startup Safety Review
 
Compliance Audits
Incident Investigation
Employee Participation
Hot Work Permits
Contractors
Emergency Planning & Response
 
 
 5.0 FIVE-YEAR ACCIDENT HISTORY
Prior to the delivery date of this document, there have been no CalARP Program-related accidents at the City of California City in the past five (5) years.  An incident investigation procedure is kept onsite, which summarizes the required data that will be used as necessary to document any CalARP Program-related incidents.
 
6.0 EMERGENCY RESPONSE PROGRAM
City of California City is committed to providing a safe and healthful work environment for its employees, the surrounding community, and the environment. The prevention of accidents, injuries, fires, emergency releases, and other emergency situations is of utmost importance and shall be the first priority for all persons working at the refinery.
City of California City is not a first responder. Thus, City of California City has an Emergency Action Plan in place and submits appropriate documentation regarding the chemicals and associated quantities to be included in the community emergency response plan.
 
7.0 PLANNED CHANGES TO IMPROVE SAFETY
The planned changes to improve safety at the facility resolve the recommendations derived from the Process Hazard Analysis, as well as incorporated recommendations from compliance audits and incident investigations, as they become available.  The facility has a tracking system for implement
ing these recommendations and ensuring its closure. As required by the regulations, recommendations will be addressed and closed in a timely manner.
